analysis: The broad option prioritises Western art history, Renaissance exchange, Greek and world archaeology, African heritage, art historiography and museums. These courses study objects, styles, material practices and contexts. Film, literary interpretation and qualitative research complement visual and cultural analysis. Building with Nature adds a concrete historical and design connection through Walcheren water management, while architectural history and restoration remain specialist gaps.

The modern option prioritises the study of modern movements, museums, adaptation, documentary, histories of gender, popular media and public communication. African heritage and museum work keep its representation and public memory questions anchored in material and institutional cases. Media analysis and historical study contribute more directly than the prior American Century research seminar.

The landscape option combines historical and material heritage with site and landscape interpretation. Building with Nature, Living with Water, Earth Observation and Spatial Planning contribute regional history, infrastructure, land-use questions and methods for reading physical landscapes. Biodiversity, climate and environmental media connect environmental change to public accounts. Indigenous ecological knowledge and sovereignty provide a contrasting way to understand land and heritage. Technical courses do not supply architectural or garden history.

The options differ by 52.5, 97.5 and 97.5 EC each way. The landscape repair replaces both conflicting courses with available study tied to landscape planning and water. The remaining replacements improve coherence by moving away from recycling, resource geoscience and general historical research. Partial landscape design, visual analysis and heritage matches leave separate rows for architectural and garden history, preservation, the practice lab, excursion and thesis.
constructionStop: Three coherent, distinct options reach the programme limit.
